PMGT1865 Week 10 - Earned Value Management (EVM)

Overview

Earned value management (EVM) measures project performance by comparing three numbers at a given status date: what was planned to be done (PV), what was actually achieved (EV), and what was actually spent (AC). It works as an early-warning system that prompts investigation and action.

• The core definitions: budget at completion (BAC), planned value (PV), earned value (EV) and actual cost (AC).

• The performance measures: cost variance (CV), schedule variance (SV), cost performance index (CPI) and schedule performance index (SPI).

• Forecasting: estimate to complete (ETC), estimate at completion (EAC) under two assumptions, and variance at completion (VAC).

• Worked examples, including a full status table for the Riverside Sounds festival project.

• When EVM can be trusted and used well: data quality, baseline integrity, and where it fits (clear, stable projects) and where it fits less well (exploratory work).

Key Concepts

What EVM does

EVM measures and reports current performance and predicts future outcomes by comparing planned work, achieved work and actual spending. It is an early-warning system: an index outside 1.0 tells you to investigate, analyse and act. It does not by itself diagnose the cause or prescribe the fix.

The four base quantities

• BAC (Budget at Completion): the total budget for the defined scope - the sum of all planned budgets for the work.

• PV (Planned Value), also BCWS (Budgeted Cost of Work Scheduled): the budgeted value of the work that was planned to be complete by the status date, taken from the time-phased budget (the cost baseline spread over time).

• EV (Earned Value), also BCWP (Budgeted Cost of Work Performed): the budgeted value of the work actually completed by the status date.

• AC (Actual Cost): what was actually spent to complete that work.

For a single activity:

• PV = BAC x planned fraction complete at the status date.

• EV = BAC x actual fraction complete at the status date.

Actual spending is not a progress measure: spending money does not prove work is done. PV, EV and AC must refer to the same scope, the same status date, the same currency, and a consistent cumulative-or-period basis.

Performance measures

Measure

Formula

Meaning

Cost variance

CV = EV - AC

Positive: completed work cost less than budgeted. Negative: over budget. Zero: on budget

Schedule variance

SV = EV - PV

Positive: ahead in budgeted work value. Negative: behind. Zero: on plan. Measured in money or work value, not in days

Cost performance index

CPI = EV / AC

Above 1 favourable, below 1 unfavourable, 1 on plan: budgeted value earned per unit of actual spend

Schedule performance index

SPI = EV / PV

Above 1 ahead, below 1 behind, 1 on plan: work value earned per unit of planned work value

Cost-weighted completion

100 x EV / BAC

Share of budgeted value earned; not the simple average of task percentages

Budget consumed

100 x AC / BAC

Share of the budget spent; not physical progress

Forecasting formulas

Situation

Formulas

Assumption

The remaining work will be done at the planned rate (a one-off "special cause" explains the variance)

ETC = BAC - EV; EAC = AC + ETC

Past deviation is not expected to repeat

The cost efficiency seen so far continues (the variance is "common cause")

ETC = (BAC - EV) / CPI; EAC = AC + ETC = BAC / CPI

The observed CPI persists to the end

Variance at completion

VAC = BAC - EAC

Negative: forecast overrun. Positive: forecast saving

ETC (Estimate to Complete) is the forecast cost of the remaining work; EAC (Estimate at Completion) is the forecast total cost of the project. Using unrounded CPI, EAC = BAC / CPI and EAC = AC + (BAC - EV)/CPI are the same number; if a rounded CPI is used they can differ slightly, so state which convention you apply and round only at presentation.

Calculation rules

• If a denominator is zero, the index is N/A - not zero, not infinity.

• Sum PV, EV and AC first, then compute project-level ratios. Never take an arithmetic average of task CPI or SPI values; averages of ratios are wrong here.

• Keep full precision through the calculation and round only for display, unless the task explicitly instructs otherwise.

Frameworks and Formulas

The measurement cycle

Fix the status date and gather, for each activity: BAC, planned percent complete, actual percent complete, and actual cost.

Compute PV = BAC x planned fraction and EV = BAC x actual fraction for each activity.

Sum PV, EV and AC across activities, then compute project CV, SV, CPI and SPI.

Interpret: variances say where you are; indices say how efficiently you got there.

Forecast ETC and EAC under a stated assumption, and compare with BAC via VAC.

Investigate causes (dependencies, permits, procurement lead times, resource problems) and act.

What SV can and cannot tell you

SV compares budgeted work value planned versus earned. It cannot tell you: the sequence of activities, which activities matter most, which are on the critical path (the chain of dependent tasks that determines the shortest project duration), how many days late the project is, whether the problem is labour or materials, or what recovery would cost. Those need schedule logic analysis alongside EVM.

Reliability and conditions of use

• EVM is only as good as the percent-complete estimates, an integrated scope, schedule and cost baseline, and timely, accurate actual-cost data. Where subcontractor payments or bonuses are tied to reported progress, scrutinise how progress is measured.

• Update estimates through approved, traceable changes - but never retroactively rewrite the baseline to hide past variance. An estimate that includes risk allowances is not padding.

• Goods to be procured are recognised in the period they are expected to be received; keep that distinct from when they are paid for in cash.

• Use committed costs as the cost basis where that is the stated convention, but do not count unperformed future commitments as completed work or as its actual cost; state whether figures cover incurred or accrued cost only.

• Do not invent scope to flatter the numbers (hollow logging), do not pad, do not manipulate the baseline retroactively. Overruns are handled through a controlled contingency drawdown, not by quietly transferring costs between accounts.

• EVM suits projects with well-defined, relatively stable scope (construction, engineering, manufacturing, repeat projects). It fits highly exploratory or ambiguous work less well, though it can still be applied to that work's stable parts or to near-term work packages.

• Measurement can be daily, weekly or monthly; increase the frequency for short, complex, high-risk phases or dispersed teams. A single index never proves a project will succeed.

Baseline, contingency and the performance BAC

Two conventions exist for project contingency (funds for identified risks) and management reserve (funds for unknown risks):

• One convention holds project contingency outside the integrated performance baseline, so the performance measurement baseline excludes it.

• The other includes project contingency inside the cost baseline (for example a cost baseline of activity budgets plus contingency), with management reserve above the baseline but inside the total project budget.

The Riverside Sounds numbers used here follow the second convention and must be used consistently: the activity-level performance BAC is AUD 540,000; project contingency AUD 40,000 sits inside the cost baseline of AUD 580,000; management reserve AUD 20,000 sits above the baseline; the authorised funding ceiling is AUD 600,000. The activity EVM table below therefore uses the AUD 540,000 BAC, not the 580,000 or 600,000 figures. Whichever convention a project adopts, state it and keep it consistent.

The business case has spent 12,000 for half its budgeted value (CV = -2,000), while the design is complete for 33,000 against a 35,000 budget (CV = +2,000). Note that a whole activity budget is not the same as its planned value at a status date: without a planned percent complete, only the budget and EV can be computed here.

Steps: CV = EV - AC = 33,149 - 32,400 = +749 (completed work came in under budget). SV = EV - PV = 33,149 - 38,269 = -5,120 (behind schedule in work value). Conclusion: a project can be under budget and behind schedule at the same time. On the standard EVM charts, CV and SV are the vertical gaps between the EV and AC curves and between the EV and PV curves - they are money gaps, not time gaps. The SV of -5,120 says nothing about which tasks are late or by how many days; the schedule logic must be examined separately.

Example 3: a running analogy for planned effort versus achieved work

Plan: train over 10 weeks, 10 km and 1.5 hours per week, so 15 hours planned in total. After 5 weeks the actual hours were 1, 0.5, 2, 1.5, 2.5 - a total of 7.5 hours, exactly half the plan - but the distances covered were 6, 3, 11, 8 and 12 km, a total of 40 km against a planned 50 km. Spending half the planned effort does not mean the programme is on track: 60 km remain in the five weeks left. Effort spent is not progress made; that is the difference between AC and EV.

How to read a row, using activity E as the example: PV = BAC x planned fraction = 105,000 x 1.00 = 105,000; EV = BAC x actual fraction = 105,000 x 0.80 = 84,000; CV = EV - AC = 84,000 - 90,000 = -6,000; SV = EV - PV = 84,000 - 105,000 = -21,000; CPI = EV / AC = 84,000 / 90,000 = 0.9333; SPI = EV / PV = 84,000 / 105,000 = 0.8000.

Project level (sum first, then compute ratios): CV = 324,650 - 337,500 = -12,850; SV = 324,650 - 371,850 = -47,200; CPI = 324,650 / 337,500 = 0.9619; SPI = 324,650 / 371,850 = 0.8731.

Interpretation:

• The project is behind schedule overall (SPI 0.8731) and the completed work is over budget (CPI 0.9619).

• Activity E has the largest work-value gap (SV -21,000) and the largest cost overrun (CV -6,000). Then I (SV -9,500, CV -2,500), H (SV -4,500, CV -1,500), F (SV -3,750 but CV +750), and L (SV -3,300, CV -1,400).

• Prioritise management attention using dependencies, permit and procurement lead times and the fixed festival weekend - not SPI alone. This table contains no critical-path information and no delay durations, so those must come from schedule analysis.

• Activities M, N and O are simply not started yet (planned and actual both zero), so CPI and SPI are N/A. That is not evidence of poor efficiency.

• Optional forecasts (each with its stated assumption): if the observed CPI persists, using the unrounded ratio gives EAC = 540,000 / (324,650 / 337,500) = about AUD 561,374; if the remaining work is done at the planned rate, EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) = 337,500 + (540,000 - 324,650) = AUD 552,850.
